Predicting 30-day hospital readmission¶

Course project — Python and scikit-learn
Joud Tutanji, Rakan Al-Shishani, Mohammad Khalil (names from the proposal).

We compare simple model families on the UCI Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset. A positive label means readmitted within 30 days. This notebook explains the implementation and displays the actual full-run artifacts, rather than hard-coding expected performance.

The full implementation is in run_experiment.py and the three short modules in readmission/. The methodology document explains deliberate simplifications from the proposal. This is an academic retrospective experiment.

1. Setup¶

Run from the repository root or the notebooks directory using the project's Python environment. If results already exist, the notebook reads them. Set RUN_FULL_EXPERIMENT=True to create a new run explicitly; this can take several minutes. The quick mode is only an installation check.

2. Dataset and target¶

Source: UCI, DOI 10.24432/C5230J, CC BY 4.0. There are 101,766 source encounters and repeated patients. We keep None in laboratory fields as “test not performed” and treat ? as missing. Death/hospice discharge codes are excluded. The labels >30 and NO both become zero.

Only deterministic, prespecified transformations happen before splitting; learned transformations happen inside pipelines.

In [2]:
import hashlib
source_path = ROOT / "data/raw/diabetic_data.csv"
assert hashlib.sha256(source_path.read_bytes()).hexdigest() == metadata["source_sha256"], "Dataset differs from the saved experiment."
raw = load_data(ROOT / "data/raw/diabetic_data.csv")
cohort = clean_cohort(raw)
X = make_features(cohort)
y = cohort["readmitted"].eq("<30").astype(int)
groups = cohort["patient_nbr"]
print(f"Raw encounters: {len(raw):,}; eligible: {len(cohort):,}")
print(f"Eligible patients: {groups.nunique():,}; prepared features: {X.shape[1]}")
display(raw["readmitted"].value_counts().rename("source_count").to_frame())
print("Lab category preserved:", "None" in raw["A1Cresult"].unique())

3. An approximately 80/20 split, then five-fold CV¶

A patient must never appear on both sides of a split. We take the first fixed fold of a seeded five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold as the test set, then form five new folds within the training portion. Proportions are approximate because patients have different numbers of encounters.

Workflow: eligible encounters → patient-disjoint train/test → training-fold preprocessing and grid search → training OOF threshold selection → freeze selection → evaluate test patients.

In [3]:
train_idx, test_idx, cv = make_splits(X, y, groups, seed=metadata["seed"], folds=5)
X_train, y_train = X.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[train_idx]
assert set(groups.iloc[train_idx]).isdisjoint(groups.iloc[test_idx])
for fit_idx, val_idx in cv:
    assert set(groups.iloc[train_idx].iloc[fit_idx]).isdisjoint(
        groups.iloc[train_idx].iloc[val_idx]
    )
audit = json.loads((RESULTS / "split_audit.json").read_text())
display(pd.DataFrame([
    {"split": "train", "encounters": audit["train_rows"], "patients": audit["train_patients"], "positive_rate": audit["train_positive_rate"]},
    {"split": "test", "encounters": audit["test_rows"], "patients": audit["test_patients"], "positive_rate": audit["test_positive_rate"]},
]))
display(pd.DataFrame(audit["cv"]))
print("Patient overlap: zero in the holdout split and all CV folds.")

5. Pipelines and model families¶

Numerical columns: median imputation and StandardScaler. Categorical columns: explicit missing category and OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"). These transformers are fitted afresh inside each CV training fold.

We compare majority baseline, ordinary and balanced logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, histogram gradient boosting, and a small one-hidden-layer MLP. Histogram boosting is the only pipeline needing dense input. The search grids are deliberately small.

6. Grid search, selection, and decision thresholds¶

The full experiment uses the following standard pattern for each family:

search = GridSearchCV(pipeline, grid, cv=cv,
    scoring={"ap": "average_precision", "roc_auc": "roc_auc"}, refit="ap")
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

For the chosen settings, fresh clones predict each training validation fold. We choose the threshold maximizing positive-class F1 on these pooled out-of-fold predictions. We freeze all thresholds and the model with the highest mean CV AP before predicting the test set.

These are development CV scores, not unbiased nested-CV estimates: the folds are reused for tuning and threshold selection. Standard deviation across folds is not a confidence interval.

7. Held-out evaluation¶

Accuracy alone can hide zero recall. Average precision (AP) is the primary selection metric; it is scikit-learn's average-precision summary, not trapezoidal PR-AUC. The positive fraction is its no-skill reference. All precision/recall/F1 values refer to the <30 class. Lower Brier score is better.

The selected model remains the CV winner even if another model happens to do better on this particular test set.

In [7]:

8. Weighting and threshold tradeoffs¶

Compare ordinary versus balanced logistic regression at 0.5, then compare each with its validation-selected threshold. Class weights affect fitting; the threshold affects which scores become positive predictions. They solve different parts of the imbalance problem. Weighted model scores can be poorly calibrated.

10. Reuse the fitted model¶

The saved artifact contains the fitted pipeline and validation-selected threshold. Apply the same deterministic feature preparation before prediction. This example uses five already evaluated test encounters for demonstration; it is not another performance estimate.

In [10]:
artifact = joblib.load(RESULTS / "models/selected_model.joblib")
example_encounters = cohort.iloc[test_idx[:5]].drop(columns="readmitted")
example_X = make_features(example_encounters)
probabilities = artifact["pipeline"].predict_proba(example_X)[:, 1]
display(pd.DataFrame({
    "encounter_id": example_encounters["encounter_id"].to_numpy(),
    "model_score": probabilities,
    "predicted_readmission": (probabilities >= artifact["threshold"]).astype(int),
}))

11. Discussion for your report¶

Use the measured numbers above to explain:

  • How the CV-selected model compares with the majority baseline.
  • Whether class weighting or threshold selection improves recall, and what happens to false alarms.
  • Why AUROC, AP, F1, and calibration tell different parts of the story.
  • Which model families work reasonably well without large searches.

Limits: historical data, no future-year or external-hospital test, repeated encounters weighted equally, sensitive attributes retained without a fairness evaluation, and no proof of clinical utility. We use a discharge-time prediction target. We simplify the proposal by using scikit-learn boosting, class weights, and a patient holdout plus ordinary grouped CV. We do not claim exact replication of published studies.

See docs/methodology.md, docs/presentation_guide.md, and results/report.md for the complete explanation and references.
